V02-A-001: A promise binds us partly because it lets another person plan around what we will do. That is why a promise cannot simply be cancelled when keeping it becomes inconvenient: the inconvenience was foreseeable, and the other person relied on us precisely so that our later moods would not matter. Yet it does not follow that every promise binds in every circumstance. If I promise to meet a friend for lunch and on the way I find a stranger injured on the road, no sensible friend would think I had wronged them by stopping. What releases me is not my changed preference but a change the promise was never meant to cover, one that both of us, had we thought of it, would have agreed to exclude. The force of a promise, then, is real but bounded by what it was understood to be about.
V02-A-002: Two pictures of moral worth pull in different directions. On one, the person who is honest only by overcoming a strong temptation to lie deserves more credit than the person to whom lying never occurs, since the first has had to do something and the second has merely been lucky in temperament. On the other, the person who must struggle reveals that part of them still wants the wrong thing, while the person for whom honesty is second nature shows what a good character actually looks like. Each picture captures something. The struggler's effort is admirable as an achievement, but we would not wish our friends to remain strugglers for ever; we hope that effort will eventually turn into ease. Effort, on this view, is the honourable path to virtue rather than its finest form.
V02-A-003: Moral philosophers often test principles against imagined cases: a runaway trolley, a surgeon with five dying patients, a drowning child beside an expensive suit. The method is defended on the ground that stripping away messy detail isolates the feature that matters. But the stripping is not neutral. A real surgeon could never be certain that the transplant would succeed, that no one would find out, or that the healthy visitor had no one depending on him; our reluctance to approve the killing may be a sound response to exactly these uncertainties, which the case asks us to set aside but which our intuitions were formed to track. When an intuition about an idealised case conflicts with a principle, it is therefore unclear which has been refuted. This does not make imagined cases useless, since they can still show that a principle has implications its defenders had not noticed; it makes them weaker as evidence against principles than they are usually taken to be.
V02-A-004: It is sometimes objected that an institution cannot meaningfully apologise for wrongs committed before any of its present members were born, since none of them did anything wrong. The objection assumes that an apology is mainly a confession of personal guilt. But an apology also does something else: it states publicly that what happened was a wrong, not a misfortune or a regrettable necessity, and it commits the speaker to a relationship in which that wrong is not repeated or excused. A university, a company or a city persists across generations precisely as the bearer of such commitments; it signs contracts that outlive its staff and honours debts its founders incurred. If it can inherit obligations of this kind, it can also inherit the duty to acknowledge what was done in its name. What it cannot do is make its present members feel personal guilt, and an apology that demands such feeling misunderstands its own purpose.
V02-A-005: Nostalgia was once treated as a kind of illness, a homesickness that weakened soldiers and emigrants. A more recent view sees it as doing useful work. People tend to become nostalgic when they feel lonely, uncertain or adrift, and the memories they return to are usually of moments shared with others: a family meal, a school trip, a celebration. Recalling such moments reminds a person that they have been valued and connected, and that sense of continuity can steady them in an unsettled present. Nostalgia is not always benign; it can harden into a refusal to accept change, or into a fantasy of a past that never was. But in its ordinary form it seems less a flight from the present than a way of drawing on the past to cope with it.
V02-A-006: When a decision turns out badly, observers tend to judge it as having been a poor decision, even when they are told exactly what the decision-maker knew at the time. A doctor whose reasonable choice of treatment is followed by a rare complication is rated as less competent than one who made the same choice and was lucky. This tendency to grade decisions by their outcomes is often described simply as an error, and in many settings it is one. Yet it is not wholly irrational. In daily life we rarely know what someone knew, and outcomes are often the only evidence we have of their judgement; a rule of thumb that trusts outcomes is a sensible response to that ignorance. The difficulty is that we go on applying the rule even when the facts that would make it unnecessary are placed in front of us.
V02-A-007: Ask people why they chose one pair of socks over another, why they liked a job candidate, why they moved house, and they will readily give reasons. It is tempting to treat these reasons as reports, read off from some inner record of what actually moved them. There is good ground for doubt. People's explanations often match what an outsider would guess, given the culture's ordinary theories of why people act, more closely than they match whatever in fact influenced the choice; and when an influence was something they did not notice, such as the position of an item on a shelf, they seldom mention it. It does not follow that people know nothing of their own minds. They are usually right about what they feel and what they are attending to. What is shaky is their access to the causes of their choices, which they seem to infer much as anyone else would, while experiencing the inference as direct knowledge.
V02-A-008: Procrastination is usually treated as a failure of time management, and the usual remedies follow from that diagnosis: calendars, lists, deadlines broken into smaller pieces. These help some people, but they often fail the chronic procrastinator, who typically knows perfectly well how much time remains and what needs to be done. A better account starts from feeling rather than scheduling. The task that is put off is usually one that provokes some discomfort, whether boredom, self-doubt or fear of being judged, and delay offers immediate relief from that discomfort at the cost of greater trouble later. Seen this way, the procrastinator is not miscalculating time but managing a mood, badly. Planning tools are not useless, but they work best when they also make the task feel less threatening, for instance by turning a vague, daunting assignment into a first step small enough to begin without dread.
V02-A-009: It is often said that public libraries have lost their purpose now that so much information can be found online. The argument mistakes what libraries do. Lending books was always only part of their role; they are also among the few indoor public places where a person may stay for hours without buying anything, where a student without a quiet room at home can study, an elderly reader can find company, and a job seeker can use a computer and ask for help. These functions have not moved online, and for people with little money or space they may matter more than ever. Libraries certainly need to change what they offer, but the case for keeping them does not rest on books alone.
V02-A-010: Jokes are notoriously the hardest thing to translate, and the reason is not simply that they rely on puns. Even a joke with no wordplay depends on what its audience already knows and expects: which professions are thought pompous, which towns are thought backward, which subjects are too serious to mention lightly. The joke works by briefly upsetting these expectations, and a listener who does not share them sees nothing upset. A translator can explain the background, but an explained joke has lost the speed on which its effect depends. The more faithful strategy is often to replace the joke with a different one that does similar work for the new audience, accepting that fidelity to the effect may require infidelity to the words.
V02-A-011: Two attitudes have long divided those who care for old buildings. One holds that a ruined church or fort should be restored to the state its builders intended, replacing lost towers and repainting faded walls, so that visitors see the work as it was meant to be seen. The other holds that such restoration is a kind of forgery: the building's age, its damage and its later alterations are part of its history, and the honest course is to stop further decay while leaving the marks of time visible. The second attitude has largely prevailed among conservation specialists, and with reason, since reconstruction often rests on guesswork about what the original looked like. Yet it is not costless. A building conserved as a fragment may be honest but unintelligible to visitors who cannot picture the whole, and some careful, clearly marked reconstruction may be the price of making the past legible.
V02-A-012: Collectors who travelled villages writing down folk songs are usually praised for saving a heritage that would otherwise have vanished. The praise is deserved, but it hides a paradox. A song in oral circulation has no single correct version: each singer alters the words, the tune and the length to suit the occasion, and this variation is not corruption but the way the tradition lives. Once a collector prints one version, often the one sung by the most cooperative informant on a particular afternoon, that version tends to become the standard, taught in schools and performed at festivals, while the others come to seem like mistakes. The act of preservation thus fixes what was fluid. None of this means collectors should have stayed at home; without them most of these songs would be lost entirely. It means that a printed collection should be read as a snapshot of a moving practice, not as the authentic original from which variants departed.
V02-A-013: Historians value memoirs for their vividness but treat them with caution, and the reasons are not mainly about honesty. A memoir is usually written long after the events, when the author knows how things turned out, and memory tends to reshape the past to fit that knowledge: doubts are forgotten, lucky guesses become foresight, and decisions made in confusion acquire a clear purpose. Memoirists also write for an audience and often to defend a reputation. None of this makes memoirs worthless. They record impressions, motives and atmosphere that official papers omit, and read alongside letters and documents from the time, they can be revealing. The caution is about using them alone as a record of what happened and why.
V02-A-014: Counterfactual history, the study of what might have happened had some event gone differently, is often dismissed as a parlour game for historians with too much time. The dismissal overlooks that every causal claim in history is already a counterfactual. To say that a drought caused a rebellion is to say that without the drought the rebellion would not have occurred, or would have come later or smaller; a historian who refuses to think about alternatives cannot weigh causes at all. The real objection is to counterfactuals that stray far from the moment in question, imagining chains of consequences decades long, where every step multiplies uncertainty. Asking what was genuinely possible for the people involved, given what they knew and could do, is not fantasy but part of explaining why events took the course they did.
V02-A-015: We tend to think of a map as a picture of what is already there, accurate or inaccurate according to how faithfully it copies the land. Many maps in history did more than copy. When a state surveyed a frontier region and drew a line across it, the line often did not record a boundary that people on the ground recognised; it created one, which taxes, passports and armies would later enforce. Rivers that had joined communities became borders that separated them. To say this is not to deny that maps can be more or less accurate about coastlines and mountains. It is to recognise that for things like boundaries, ownership and jurisdiction, the map was frequently an instrument for making the world rather than a record of it.
V02-A-016: Historians have learned to read archives not only for what they say but for what they leave out. An archive is the residue of an administration's interests: it keeps tax rolls, court cases and correspondence among officials, and so it records people mainly when they paid, offended or petitioned. Whole areas of life, such as household work, friendship and private belief, appear only when they collided with authority. It has become common to conclude that the archive simply silences the powerless. That conclusion goes too far. The same court records that reduce a person to a defendant often preserve, in the words of witnesses, details of daily life recorded nowhere else, and a petition written to flatter an official can still reveal what its writer wanted. The archive is biased in what it selects, but read against its grain it yields more about ordinary lives than its makers ever intended.
V02-A-017: Loyalty programmes look like a gift: buy nine coffees and the tenth is free. For the seller, the point is less the discount than the switching cost it creates. A customer who is halfway to a reward has a reason to return to the same shop even when another is closer or cheaper, because going elsewhere means abandoning the progress already made. The programme also gives the seller information about what customers buy and how often, which can be used to target offers. Customers are not necessarily fooled; many value the rewards and would shop in the same place anyway. But the programme is designed mainly to make leaving a little more expensive than staying.
V02-A-018: A price of zero is not just a very low price. People respond to free offers far more strongly than a small drop in price would predict: a product reduced from a small sum to nothing attracts many more takers than one reduced by the same amount to a slightly smaller sum. One reason is that a free choice seems to carry no possible loss, so the usual weighing of costs and benefits is skipped. This is why many online services charge nothing and earn their revenue from advertising or data instead. The user does pay, in attention and in information about themselves, but these costs are spread out and hard to count, and so they do not trigger the caution that a visible price, however small, would.
V02-A-019: Open-plan offices were promoted on the promise that removing walls would bring colleagues together and multiply the chance conversations from which ideas emerge. When companies have tracked what actually happens after such a move, the picture has often been the reverse: people conscious of being overheard send more messages and speak less face to face, wearing headphones to create the privacy that walls once gave. It would be wrong, however, to conclude that open plans always reduce collaboration. Teams whose work requires constant quick coordination, such as a newsroom or a trading floor, may genuinely benefit. The lesson is that physical closeness does not by itself produce interaction; whether it does depends on what the work requires and on whether people feel free to talk without being observed.
V02-A-020: In many markets, small traders lend goods to one another on credit without any written contract, and the arrangement works far better than an outsider might expect. The reason is that these traders deal with each other repeatedly and talk constantly. A trader who fails to repay does not merely lose one partner; word spreads, and soon no one in the market will extend credit to them. The threat of losing that reputation enforces the debt more cheaply than a court could. The system has limits. It works only within a community dense enough for news to travel, and it tends to exclude newcomers, who have no reputation to lose and therefore little to offer as security.
V02-A-021: National income accounts leave out the cooking, cleaning and care done unpaid within households, and the omission is often called a simple bias that a better statistic would correct. The criticism is right that something valuable goes unmeasured, and that this can distort judgements: when a family starts paying for childcare it once provided itself, measured output rises though little more care may be given. But the remedy is less simple than it sounds. To add household work to the accounts one must price it, and every method of pricing an hour of unpaid care, whether at what a hired carer would earn or at what the carer could have earned elsewhere, imposes a market valuation on activity whose meaning to those who do it is often precisely that it is not done for money. The omission is a real flaw, but the obvious fix may trade one distortion for another.
V02-A-022: Any species that arrives in a new region with human help is now often labelled invasive and treated as a threat to be removed. Some newcomers deserve that reputation: a predator introduced to an island can wipe out birds that evolved without defences against it. But many introduced plants and animals settle in without causing measurable harm, and some come to fill roles left empty by the loss of native species, providing food for pollinators or shelter for birds. Judging a species by its origin rather than its effects can waste money on removing harmless arrivals while drawing attention from the damaging ones. The useful question is not where a species came from but what it actually does.
V02-A-023: Journals are more likely to publish studies that find an effect than studies that find none, and researchers, knowing this, are less likely to write up their null results at all. Each choice seems reasonable, since a finding that nothing happened looks less interesting than a discovery. Together, however, they distort the record. If twenty teams test a useless remedy and one obtains a positive result by chance, that one study may be the only one anyone reads, and the remedy will appear to work. The problem lies not in any single dishonest scientist but in a system that filters results by whether they are exciting rather than by whether they are sound.
V02-A-024: Two strategies compete for the limited money available to protect plant diversity. Seed banks store frozen samples of thousands of species in secure vaults, offering insurance against extinction at modest cost. Conservation in the wild protects plants where they grow, along with the insects, fungi and soils they depend on. The seed bank's great advantage is security, but its samples are frozen in time: a population kept in a vault stops adapting to changing climate and pests, and some species have seeds that cannot survive drying and freezing at all. Wild populations go on evolving, but they are exposed to every threat the vault avoids. Neither strategy can substitute for the other. The vault is best understood as a backup for living populations, not a replacement for them.
V02-A-025: Naturalists have long divided into those who tend to lump similar organisms into one broad species and those who split them into many narrow ones. The dispute is often presented as a quarrel of temperaments, as if one side were simply careless and the other fussy. In fact it reflects something real about living things. Populations diverge gradually, and at any moment some pairs are clearly distinct, some clearly the same, and many lie in between, interbreeding a little or differing in a few traits. For these intermediate cases no fact of nature settles whether there are one species or two; the answer depends on which criterion one adopts. This does not make classification arbitrary, since the clear cases are clear. But it means that some disputes about species are disagreements about definitions rather than about the organisms.
